title: Research
text:
My research sits between stellar astrophysics and astroinformatics. I am interested in how massive stars live and die, and in building statistical and machine-learning tools for the large data sets that surveys such as ZTF and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory (LSST) are producing. Below are the three projects I am working on. All of them are still in progress and not yet published, so this page gives only a general picture. More details will come once the papers are out.

  
  
    PhD thesis · in preparation
    Multimodal deep learning for supernovae
    Most methods that classify and characterize transients use only light curves. In my thesis, supervised by Dr. Francisco Förster, I am building a variational autoencoder that learns from light curves and spectra together. The model encodes each supernova in a latent space whose coordinates have a physical meaning, and decodes it into a spectral energy distribution that can be compared directly with the observations. It extends the ParSNIP model (Boone 2021) and uses ZTF photometry from the ALeRCE broker and spectra from WISeREP. It is written in PyTorch and trained on high-performance computing clusters.
  



  
  
    Paper in preparation
    The transition phase of Type II supernovae
    After the plateau, the light curves of hydrogen-rich (Type II) supernovae drop quickly before they settle onto the radioactive tail. This short transition phase has received much less attention than the plateau or the tail. With Dr. Claudia P. Gutiérrez, Dr. Santiago González-Gaitán and Dr. Laureano Martinez, I characterize this transition in a large sample of observed supernovae using an analytic model and Bayesian (MCMC) fitting. We then compare the observations with hydrodynamical explosion models to learn what the transition can tell us about the progenitor star and the explosion.
  



  
  
    Ongoing
    Sulfur-bearing molecules in IRC+10216
    IRC+10216 is the nearest carbon-rich AGB star and one of the richest chemical laboratories in the sky. I combine quantum-chemistry calculations (structures, energies and spectroscopic constants of isomers) with millimeter observations from the APEX telescope to search for new sulfur-bearing molecules in its circumstellar envelope, such as HCSCN, HCSCCH and c-C2H2S. I have presented this work at the Chilean Astrochemistry School and at the 1st Colombian Symposium on Astrochemistry.
  

If you want to know more or would like to collaborate, write to me at sjurado@das.uchile.cl.

 Astroinformatics & Astrostatistics. Machine learning and deep learning applied to astronomical data; multimodal generative models; classification and characterization of transient events; large-scale data analysis.

title: Bryam Steve Pinilla Jurado
text:
Research Experience
 2024 – Present | Doctoral research — Multimodal classification of transients | Universidad de Chile, Santiago, Chile.

Extension of a variational autoencoder architecture (ParSNIP, Boone 2021) to incorporate multimodality, a novel feature in this research area. Construction of the full data pipeline: ingestion of light curves from the ALeRCE broker and of spectra from the WISeREP database, with preprocessing, smoothing and filtering of irregular time series. Implemented in PyTorch on HPC infrastructure. Developed in consultation with Prof. Andrew Connolly (University of Washington; Director of the eScience Institute and of DiRAC).

 2023 – Present | Astrochemistry — Sulfur-bearing molecules in IRC+10216 | Universidad de Chile, Santiago, Chile.

Computational and observational search for sulfur-bearing molecules (HCSCN, HCSCCH, c-C2H2S) around the carbon star IRC+10216, using data from the APEX telescope.

 2022 – 2024 | Junior Researcher | Fundación Universidad del Valle — Macondo Astronomy & Astrophysics Group (GAAM), Cali, Colombia | Collaboration with Dr. Lauren Flor-Torres and Dr. Camilo Delgado-Correal.
 2021 – 2022 | RECA Research Internship | International collaboration, Remote.

Statistical characterization of the transition phase in the light curves of hydrogen-rich supernovae, to constrain their progenitors and explosion properties. Parameter estimation carried out within a Bayesian framework using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling, including posterior inference and uncertainty quantification. Supervised by Dr. Claudia P. Gutiérrez (Universitat de Barcelona) and Dr. Santiago González-Gaitán (CENTRA, Universidade de Lisboa).

 2021 | Project Leader — 100 Hours 100 Schools | IASC / Las Cumbres Observatory, Remote.

Coordination of allocated observing time (90-minute blocks yielding 7–9 images per target) and delivery of analysis sessions on deep-sky objects, planets and minor bodies with school students.
